title: CoMAS: Co-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems via Interaction Rewards
one_liner: LLM agents improve themselves by learning from how well they work together, measured by scoring each other's contributions.
lead: When you have multiple AI assistants working on a task together, they can teach each other to get better because each one sees the other's reaction in real time, which reveals what works and what does not. This paper shows how to measure the quality of their teamwork automatically (by having a third LLM score each turn) and use that signal to improve each agent's strategy, all without anyone writing reward rules by hand.

problem.h2: Agents learn the old way: from labels or dense scores
paras: Today's AI assistants (large language models, or LLMs) are trained once and then frozen. A naive next step is to have them keep learning after deployment: improve on new tasks because each one must adapt to different real-world uses, get better at your specific job because the general model has not seen your exact setup, and adapt over time because the world changes.

Current methods either require a human to label every output as good or bad (dense external feedback), or they try to invent a reward signal by asking the LLM itself to score its own work. But humans do not actually learn this way: you learn by talking with others, seeing where they disagree with you, and refining your approach through that back-and-forth.

callout.html: Multiple agents discuss a problem together, score each other's contributions during the conversation (because each agent's words either helped or hindered progress, and a judge can spot that), and use those scores to improve their strategies without external labels (because reinforcement learning lets them learn from any reward signal, not just human approval).

panels.title: 1. Setup: Two agents on a task
panels.caption: Agent A and Agent B work on the same problem together.

panels.title: 2. Problem: One agent talks, the other learns nothing
panels.caption: Without feedback, Agent A has no way to know if its response was good.

panels.title: 3. Interaction: Agents discuss and critique
panels.caption: Agent A makes a proposal, Agent B critiques it, A refines. A sees live reaction.

panels.title: 4. Scoring happens inside the conversation
panels.caption: Judge scores each agent's move. A sees that thoughtful moves score higher.

panels.title: 5. Payoff: Agents refine strategies based on scores
panels.caption: Over time, agents learn which conversation moves yield higher scores.

steps.text: Create two or more LLM agents, each with their own learned strategy for how to respond in a conversation.
Agents take turns proposing ideas or critiques on a shared problem; each response is a concrete utterance.
After each turn, another LLM (the judge) reads the full conversation so far and scores how well that turn contributed to progress.
Each agent's own move gets a score; that score is the intrinsic reward signal for that agent's action.
Each agent uses standard reinforcement learning (a method for rewarding good decisions) to nudge its weights so higher-scoring moves become more likely.

object.h2: What the paper changes: internal agent weights driven by interaction scores
paras: Every LLM is a collection of numbers (weights) that control what the model says next. This paper tunes those weights to maximize the score the agent receives during teamwork, instead of trying to score itself or waiting for external labels.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: contribution quality, measured live during conversation
hidden.name: Interaction score (quality of each agent's turn)
paras: The paper needs a way to know whether an agent's move was good or bad in the moment, without a human saying so. It invents a measurement: after each agent speaks, a judge LLM reads the conversation and assigns a score to that turn—a number from, say, 0 to 10 indicating how much that move helped the team make progress.

This score is invisible in normal conversation but central to learning: the agent collects its scores over many conversations, and reinforcement learning uses them to steer future behavior. High-scoring moves (crisp clarifications, sharp critiques, unexpected suggestions) become more probable; low-scoring moves (repetition, irrelevant tangents) fade.

heat.caption: Darker means higher judge score; agent learns to repeat the bright behaviors.

reads.html: The judge is watching how each agent's words affect the conversation. It asks: Does this move clarify the problem? Does it point out a real flaw? Does it move the group closer to a solution? A good move gets a high score.

The paper calls this the 'interaction reward' signal. It emerges from the back-and-forth of the discussion, where agents build on each other's ideas—not from the agent judging itself, and not from a human labeler, but from an external LLM observing the multi-agent interaction and scoring contributions.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: learning from live feedback on collaborative behavior
paras: The mechanism has three steps. First, the conversation itself creates a natural signal: when two agents interact, one agent's move either helps or hinders the other because each utterance either adds clarity or adds noise. A clarifying question unblocks progress because the other agent can now act on solid footing; a contradictory statement causes confusion because the other agent must now reconcile conflicting instructions. This ground truth is observable in the conversation's trajectory because you can see whether the agents move forward together or loop back to explain things.

Second, the judge scores each move, grounding that observation as a number. Because the judge has read the full context of the conversation, it can recognize what actually moved things forward versus what wasted time.

Third, reinforcement learning works by rewarding actions that raise a score, which means the algorithm nudges the weights in whichever direction makes good actions more likely next time. Here, an agent that receives high scores for speaking clearly and building on others' ideas will gradually shift its internal weights to emit similar utterances in similar situations because each reinforcement step adjusts the weights slightly toward the pattern. Over many conversations, those high-scoring behaviors crystallize into the agent's strategy because the weights converge to a local peak where that style is most rewarded. The process mirrors how humans improve: you notice in conversation what lands well and what flops because you see the reaction, and you unconsciously shift your approach because your brain reinforces the moves that worked.

stages.s: RL nudges weights to repeat high-scoring behaviors

math.h2: Equation: updating weights by rewarding good turns
math.words: Update each weight in a direction that increases the probability of high-scoring actions; the strength of the update grows with the score; penalize each update slightly to avoid wild changes.
math.equation: grad_theta log(pi(a_t | s_t)) * R_t - beta * KL(pi_new || pi_old)
symbols: which way to nudge the weight so the chosen action becomes more likely
the actual thing the agent said at turn t
the conversation state (everything said so far)
the judge's score for that turn (the interaction reward)
a penalty that prevents the updated strategy from drifting too far from the original

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Agent A proposes an idea that the judge scores 8 out of 10.
The base update is: (nudge direction to make that utterance more likely) * 8.
The KL penalty is: 0.1 * (distance between the new and old strategy) to keep the strategy stable.
Net effect: Agent A's weight shifts to favor similar moves, but only by a reasonable margin (not a wild swing).
Suppose Agent A says something harmful, scored 2 out of 10. The update is (nudge) * 2, nearly flat—the weights barely move, so harmful moves stay rare.

math.note: The interaction reward from the judge is the key difference: it comes from the judge, not from the agent itself or an external labeler, and it scores the whole turn in context.

bars.h2: Comparison: agents trained with interaction rewards vs. untrained

charts.title: Untrained agents (baseline)
charts.note: Agents cannot improve because no reward signal tells them what to do differently; without feedback, their weights have no direction to move.

charts.title: CoMAS (this paper)
charts.note: Agents improve over time because judge scores drive learning; better collaboration and task success.

items.html: If the judge uses a simple heuristic (e.g., rewards the longest responses), agents will learn to ramble instead of being concise. Misaligned scoring opens a loop where agents optimize the wrong thing.
If all agents converge to the same strategy (e.g., all adopt the same aggressive tone), they stop challenging each other and the feedback loop stalls. Diversity of agents is a hidden requirement.

The judge must score immediately or the connection between the agent's move and the score blurs. If scoring happens only at the end of a long conversation, the agent will not learn which specific turns were good.

The paper tests scaling to more agents and finds it works, but each additional agent means more compute for the judge. The overhead is linear, not exponential, so scalability is plausible if the judge is efficient.

The judge is an LLM, not a human. If what the judge considers good differs from what humans actually value, agents will learn the wrong thing because reinforcement learning optimizes for the reward signal it receives, whatever that signal measures. Regular audits of judge scores against human feedback help catch drift because you can spot when the judge's scores diverge from human judgment and retrain the judge if needed.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple two-agent system on a concrete problem: for example, agents collaborate to write a plan or solve a logic puzzle. Each agent proposes a step, the other comments, they refine. A judge LLM scores each contribution. Run 100 rounds of conversation, collecting scores. Train both agents' weights using standard RL to maximize interaction rewards. Measure: (1) average judge score per turn over the 100 rounds; (2) task success rate (did they arrive at the right answer?) before and after learning; (3) the number of turns to convergence.
demo.closing: The demo must show that both agents improve their scores over time because reinforcement learning is steering their weights toward high-scoring behavior, and that tasks are solved faster and more accurately after learning because better collaboration strategies mean fewer false starts and dead ends.

note_on_method: This spec was written from the paper's abstract, as the full paper is not available on arXiv. The mechanism is inferred from the abstract and theme; the math formula is a standard policy-nudging structure (nudging weights in a direction that raises the probability of good actions), adapted to this paper's interaction-reward setting. The worked example is illustrative and does not represent measured results.
